We make these claims of the Bible because of the claims made in Scripture itself. The clause “the Lord said” or its equivalent occurs 3,800 times in the Old Testament alone. God commanded the Scripture writers to write the message that He revealed. Absolute authority is claimed for the law and the testimony (Deuteronomy 28:58; Psalm 19:7; 119:142; Isaiah 8:20). Jesus and the apostles in the New Testament recognized the Old Testament as fully inspired. The Lord observed it in His teachings and in the reading in the synagogue worship. The apostles appealed to the Old Testament in the narratives of the Gospels and Acts. Peter recognized the writings of Paul to be on a level with the Old Testament (2 Peter 3:15, 16).

The nature of God as personal God and of humanity as personal creature indicates that the revelation of God by means of His Word is reasonable. God is personal, intelligent, volitional, loving, and capable of fellowship. Human beings, in the image of God, possess the same personal characteristics; in humanity, these characteristics are needs because of the dependent nature as creature. So, we raise the question: Is it not reasonable that God would speak to the creature which He made in His own image? That God would have His human servants commit that speech (revelation) to writing is also reasonable in order to preserve and protect the record for others.
By committing the record to written form, God protects it from loss and adulteration by faulty memory, intrusion of purely oral tradition, and corruptions made on the basis of experience.

The nature of Scripture is supportive of this doctrine. In one sense, the Bible is one book, but in another sense, it is sixty-six books. These books were written by more than 40 different human authors. From Moses (who wrote Genesis) to John (who wrote the last books of the Bible—The Gospel of John, the Epistles of John, and Revelation); there is a span of more than 1,500 years. Yet, for all of this diversity in authorship and spread of time, there is such a unity in the Bible that it can be regarded as one book. This unity shows up in many areas—the doctrine of God, the doctrine of salvation, the doctrine of humanity, the doctrine of eternal destiny, and the plan of the ages. Many who do not recognize the Bible as infallible will acknowledge these elements of unity. Any degree of unity under these circumstances must appeal to a divine source for authority and revelation.

There are certain doctrines in Scripture which people consistently attempt to ignore or alter. In their own humanly-made religious and philosophical systems, human beings consistently reject these doctrines. The Bible never excuses sin; it offers forgiveness. Human writings tend to substitute excuses for sin instead of forgiveness; they usually excuse or ignore sin in their heroes. They offer forgiveness through good works instead of forgiveness as a gift.

The Bible denounces all human merit in relation to salvation. Human religious systems build on good works for salvation. In this same relationship, the Bible makes faith the only instrument of salvation. This faith is the gift of God. So humankind is removed from a central position, and Christ is placed in the central position. Human systems allow man to achieve salvation by means of good works, merit of birth, and merit of station in life.
The Bible has a single moral standard—the holiness of God. Human systems tend to make holiness relative; they do not demand perfection.

The Bible condemns the sinner to hell and defines hell in terms of everlasting punishment in the flames of the lake of fire; it holds out no hope of deliverance either by annihilation or escape. Human literature avoids such a doctrine of punishment; there are doctrines of punishment in human systems, but normally they do not deal with it from the standpoint of the Bible. They avoid the doctrine of hell or make it temporal.

We do not offer these arguments from the standpoint of proving a mathematical equation, but from the standpoint of showing the reasonableness of our faith. Again, we do not offer these evidences in an attempt to substitute them for spiritual experience in faith. The persuasion of the heart and mind and the capture of the will by the Holy Word and the agency of the Holy Spirit are the real persuasions of the inspiration of the Scriptures.

These matters are pertinent to the life of the church. We must be governed by Scripture in our decisions. The Bible must be regarded as the only infallible rule of faith and practice. All church government must be based on the Word of God. All the tenets of our faith must be drawn from Scripture.
Article 2
We believe in one God eternally existing in three persons;
namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

There is one indivisible, unlimited personal being—God. The essential nature of the one God may be identified and known by the incommunicable attributes. These are qualities that cannot be shared with any creature. They are God’s self-existence, His unchangeableness, and His infinity (unlimitedness). The personal nature of the one God may be identified and known by the communicable attributes. These are qualities that may, at God’s will, be shared with and transferred to the creature. These qualities are His intellectual nature, His volitional nature (that is, His possession of a will), and His moral nature—truthfulness, holiness, justice, love, and righteousness.

There are three eternal and unchangeable personal distinctions in the Godhead; namely, the person of God the Father, the person of God the Son, and the person of God the Holy Spirit. The person of the Father is distinct from the other persons of the Godhead because He is eternally Father by having begotten the Son from eternity. The person of the Son is distinct from the other persons of the Godhead because He is eternally Son by having been begotten of the Father from eternity. The person of the Holy Spirit is distinct from the other persons of the Godhead because He is eternally Spirit of God, Spirit of the Father, and Spirit of the Son, and has from eternity proceeded from the Father and the Son.

All of the qualities of divine nature belong to each of the persons of the Trinity so that it may be said that the Father is infinite, eternal, and unchangeable; the Son is infinite, eternal, and unchangeable; and the Spirit is infinite, eternal, and unchangeable. The divine nature cannot be divided; the persons of the Godhead are one undivided and indivisible divine nature. They are the same in substance and are equal in power, glory, and honor.
They eternally exist as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as relates to their persons and as one God as relates to the divine nature.

Before we attempt an explanation of this doctrine, we should determine if it is Scriptural. It has been attacked in every age of the church, yet it is traceable to the earliest days of church history. The oldest creed of the church (as distinct from biblical quotation) contains the affirmation of the doctrine of the Trinity.

The earliest indications of the doctrine of the Trinity appear in the Old Testament. The New Testament elaborates what the Old Testament began to reveal. In a review of the Scripture’s statements on the doctrine of the Trinity, we should be aware of the two facets of this doctrine: unity of God and triune personal nature of God. Many of the Scriptures will embody both of these points; others will speak of one or the other.
The following quotations emphasize the oneness of God:
Deuteronomy 6:4: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord.”
1 Kings 8:60: Solomon prayed “that all the people of the earth may know that the Lord is
God, and that there is none else.”
1 Corinthians 8:4: “…we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none
other God but one.”
1 Corinthians 8:6: “But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and
we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.”
1 Timothy 2:5: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man
Christ Jesus.”
James 2:19: “Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe,
and tremble.”

The doctrine of the unity of God is necessary. If we believe that God is before all things, there can be only one Being who is before all other existence. If we believe that God is beyond measurement, there can be but one Being who is immeasurable (that is, infinite). If we believe that God is all-powerful, there can be no one else as powerful as He, and none can be more powerful. If we believe that God is eternal, there can be no being in existence prior to His existence; there is no existence prior to His.
We note now the Scriptures that deal with the plurality (the triune personal nature) in the Godhead:
Genesis 1:1: “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.” (The plural word

“Elohim” [gods] is used here to refer to God. We must be careful not to overstate the argument here. This does not prove Trinity, but it carries the implication of Trinity that would be developed by further revelation.)
Genesis 1:26: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” (Here
the plurality is stated by God in the plural pronouns “us” and “our.”)
Genesis 11:7: “Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language…” (In verses

eight and nine, it is said that the “Lord scattered them,” and that the “Lord confounded their language.” Clearly, the plural “us” in verse seven is fulfilled in the singular “Lord” in verses eight and nine. In this counsel, God is not conferring with angels, but within the communion of the Trinity.)
Psalm 45:6, 7: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is
a right sceptre. Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.”
Hebrews 1:8 is a quotation of Psalm 45:6, 7 in application to Christ. God, the Father,
addresses the Son and calls Him “God,” ascribes eternity to Him, and speaks of His anointing with the Holy Spirit.
Isaiah 48:16: “…and now the Lord God, and his Spirit, hath sent me.”
John 3:16: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that
whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.”
Galatians 4:4: “But when the fullness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made
of a woman, made under the law.”
John 14:26: “But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in
my name, he shall teach you all things.”
John 15:26 “But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father,
even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me.”
Mark 1:11: (and parallels) “And there came a voice from heaven, saying, Thou art my
beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
Romans 8:27: “And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit,
because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God.”
1 Corinthians 2:10: “But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit
searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God.”
Matthew 28:19: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the
Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.”
2 Corinthians 13:14: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the
communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.”

The doctrine of the Trinity is important in divine worship. The last two Scripture passages cited above illustrate this principle of worship. When we baptize in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, we recognize these three Persons as being equal in the divine formula (which is a prayer). We worship God in Trinity and in unity.

In the benediction of 2 Corinthians 13:14, we also worship God in Trinity and unity. When we pray “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” we worship the Son as the dispenser of a divine gift, namely His grace. When we pray “the love of God,” we address the Father in worship and seek Him as the source of all goodness and love. When we pray “the communion of the Holy Ghost,” we worship the Spirit whose presence and work are essential to our partaking of divine blessings and fellowship. In this benediction, we are offering prayer to each of the persons of the Godhead as individual Persons and to God in unity.
Article 3
We believe that Jesus Christ is the only begotten Son of the Father,
conceived of the Holy Ghost, and born of the Virgin Mary.
That Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised from the dead.
That He ascended to heaven and is today
at the right hand of the Father as the Intercessor.

We believe that Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God (having been begotten of the Father from eternity, identical in glory, power, and all divine attributes with the Father) and that He is the only begotten Son of God. He became a man (without any change in His divine nature) by the conception of God the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary. The divine nature and the human nature were united in one Person—Jesus of Nazareth—without any admixture or confusion of the divine nature with the human nature or the human nature with the divine. Jesus Christ was and continues to be wholly God and wholly man in two distinct natures and one Person forever.

Jesus Christ is the only Redeemer. He redeems by the fulfilling of the redemptive offices of Prophet, Priest, and King. As Prophet, He ministers by His Word and Spirit. As Priest, He offers Himself by the eternal Spirit as the only sacrifice for sins, and He makes everlasting intercession. As King, He calls, defends, protects, and perfects the kingdom of God and presents it to the Father in the reconciliation of all things.

There are three major fields of doctrine taught in this statement: (1) the nature of Christ, (2) the character of the redemption which Christ purchased, and (3) the nature of Christ’s present ministry.
Concerning the nature of Christ, we are taught two things: (1) that He is divine, and (2) that He is human. We will deal with these separately and in the order mentioned.

The divine nature of Christ is clearly taught in Scripture. He is called God (John 1:1-14; Romans 9:5; Philippians 2:5-11; Hebrews 1:8). He is described as having divine attributes. He knows all things (omniscient: John 2:24, 25; 16:30; 21:17; Colossians 2:3). He is everywhere in His divine nature (omnipresent: Matthew 18:20; John 3:13; 14:20, 23; Ephesians 1:23). He is eternal (Micah 5:2; John 1:1-14; Colossians 1:17). He is unchangeable (Hebrews 13:8). He performs divine works, which are works that can be done only by God. These works are creation (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:10), forgiveness of sins (Mark 2:5-10), judgment (John 5:22, 23; Romans 14:10; 2 Timothy 4:1), imparting of eternal life to believers (John 10:28; 17:2). He is worshiped by both humans and angels (John 5:23; Philippians 2:10, 11; Hebrews 1:6).

The human nature of Christ came from His mother, the Virgin Mary. The work of the Holy Spirit in Jesus’ miraculous conception was to act upon the human nature of the virgin and cause her to conceive a Son, and at the same time to preserve her virginity. The purity of Jesus from sin in His birth is attributable to the fact that He was conceived of the Holy Spirit and not to the purity of His mother.

The birth of our Lord must lie in the realm of the miraculous. At the same time, we must understand that the Child that was produced of this birth was human, though in His personal being He was joined with the nature of God.

The human nature of Christ is confirmed in many places in Scripture. He was made of a woman and brought under the law (Galatians 4:4). Even after His ascension, He is referred to as “the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). He had the weaknesses normally associated with human frailty: He became weary (John 4:6); He became hungry and thirsty (Matthew 21:18; John 19:28). He was mortal and subject to death (Philippians 2:8; Hebrews 2:9).
He must be God in order to enter into the presence of God, have access to the powers of divine nature, and be able to unite us to God.

It was necessary for Him to be man in order that He might experience the feeling of our infirmities, be tempted in all points as we are, enter into punishment for our sins, fulfill righteousness for us as human beings, and offer sacrifices for us as High Priest.

The union of these two natures in one Person is necessary. The Redeemer must be both God and man in order that He might be the Mediator between God and humanity. By the miracle of the virgin birth through the work of the Holy Spirit “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). God thus joined together the two natures—God and humankind—in such a perfect manner that the one Person, Jesus of Nazareth, was fully God and fully man. By bringing the two natures together in one Person, God brings the two parties together. The powers of the divine nature and the perfection of the human nature are brought together in one act of redemption.
The next area of consideration in this article of faith is the redemption that Christ accomplished. The two main emphases of this discussion are the crucifixion and the resurrection of Christ.

The crucifixion of our Lord was the end of the process of His entire earthly life. From the moment of His conception in the womb of the Virgin, He had been representative of all humankind. He was then, as now, the last man Adam. As the first man Adam had represented us in the Fall and in sin, so Christ represented us in obedience and holiness. He fulfilled obedience and holiness as the last man Adam in order to restore us to the righteousness which Adam had forfeited. All the events of this representative life led to the cross. These events consist of the fulfilling of the law. Christ was blameless before the law in order that we might have the righteousness of the law given to our credit. We could not keep the law; so, Christ kept it for us.

Christ’s personal perfection under the law could not prevail for us as long as there was the sentence of death upon us; so, the crucifixion of Christ was necessary. The justice of God (the divine judgment) must be satisfied. Since the sin was ours, the judgment was against us. It is under these circumstances that Christ presents His perfect fulfillment of righteousness on our behalf. He presents this righteousness of His life through His death on the cross. In the cross, He fulfills our punishment and satisfies the judgment of God. Christ’s death was more than simply an agonizing physical ordeal; it was the penalty of the law which was justly warranted on humankind.
We affirm the above interpretation by the following Scripture references.
Romans 4:23-25: “Now it was not written for his (Abraham’s) sake alone, that it was

imputed to him; but for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.”
Romans 5:9, 10: “Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved
from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.”
Romans 5:17-19: “For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they

which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ. Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.”
2 Corinthians 5:18, 19: “And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself

by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; to wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation.”
2 Corinthians 5:21: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we
might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Hebrews 2:16-18: “For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him

the seed of Abraham. Wherefore in all things it behooved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.”

The above is the doctrinal meaning of the crucifixion. We now look at the physical side of Christ’s death. Jesus died in the flesh; His death was neither a myth nor a fabrication. Jesus of Nazareth literally died by means of the crucifixion. He was buried, and He remained in the tomb for three days. He was treated as any other corpse would have been under the circumstances. This emphasis on the literalness of Christ’s death determines our understanding of the Resurrection.

The resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was literal; that is, it was a resurrection of the body. It occurred on the third day after His crucifixion. This event is historical. The Resurrection was not the revival of a body from a faint. Neither was it a myth nor any other kind of fabrication. The same body that was placed in the tomb came out of the tomb resurrected to everlasting glory. The resurrected body could be seen and touched. It was prepared to enter into heaven because it had become immortal and glorious. It is important that we understand these points, because they are fundamental to the scriptural understanding of the Resurrection.
The Resurrection teaches us certain things about Christ. The Resurrection is the Father’s seal of approval upon Christ personally and upon His life and death. It testifies that the Father

has accepted Christ’s satisfaction of divine judgment in the act of the Cross. The Resurrection is Christ’s victory over sin and death. Through the Resurrection, Christ is set forth in His lordship over the living and the dead. The Resurrection is the Holy Spirit’s declaration that Jesus is the Son of God.
Luke 24:39: “Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a
spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.”
1 Corinthians 15:3, 4: “For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how
that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.”
1 Timothy 3:16: “And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was
manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.”
Romans 1:3, 4: “Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the seed
of David according to the flesh; and declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead.”

The Resurrection teaches us certain things about our own experience and hope. In His resurrection, Christ acted as the last man Adam—the representative person for us. He stood as the head of His church, and as such He accomplished the redemption and victory of the church. By the resurrection of Christ, believers have their justification, spiritual quickening, victory over their enemies, and assurance of their own personal resurrection.
The third area of doctrine represented in this statement of faith is the present ministry of Christ. This ministry is being conducted by Christ, who is at the Father’s right hand in heavenly places.

By His ascension, Christ was lifted above all principalities and powers and placed at God’s right hand. This event took place forty days after the Resurrection; it took place at the Mount of Olives and was witnessed by His disciples. It was a miraculous event in which Jesus was bodily lifted out of this realm of existence and into heaven. The Ascension is the pattern by which we anticipate the return of our Lord.
Luke 24:51: “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and
carried up into heaven.”
Acts 1:9-11: “And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken

up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. And while they looked steadfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel; which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? This same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.”
The doctrinal significance of the Ascension is essential to our doctrine of Christ. This event was the Father’s exaltation of the Son to the right hand of power. This demonstrates the Son’s
supremacy and victory over all principalities and powers. It shows Christ’s headship over the church.
Ephesians 1:19-23: “And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who

believe, according to the working of his mighty power, which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come: and hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him that filleth all in all.”
In His redemptive provisions, Christ serves us as Prophet, Priest, and King. He has ascended into heaven to serve in these roles at the Father’s right hand.

As Prophet, He reveals the will of God to us. He himself is the Word of God and the sender of the Holy Spirit to reveal God and the will of God. By the Holy Spirit, He has given all Scripture through the Holy Spirit’s inspiration. He provides the prophetic ministry to the church through the ministers of the Word and through the ministries of the Holy Spirit in the interpretation of tongues and in prophecies.

As Priest, our Lord has ascended into the heavenly Holy of Holies and to the heavenly altar to offer His blood for our atonement. Through Him, our sacrifices of worship (praise, prayer, giving, obedience, spiritual living, etc.) are offered to the Father. He receives the gifts of God for us and bestows them upon the believers; the Holy Ghost is such a gift, as are the offices of the church. He makes everlasting intercession for us.

As King, Christ is presently sitting at the right hand of power and is ruling in His kingdom particularly and in the world generally. In His rulership over the world, Christ is Creator and Sustainer of all the realms of creaturehood. He is directing them in order that all things will glorify Him. In His rulership in the Kingdom which has been purchased by His blood, Christ is bringing the believers into subjection to the will of God and protecting them against their enemies. He will return to climax His earthly reign in the Millennium and the heavenly reign in the new heaven and the new earth.
Article 4
We believe that all have sinned and come short of the glory of God
and that repentance is commanded of God for all
and necessary for forgiveness of sins.

In the first man Adam, all those who would descend from him by ordinary human procreation sinned. The entire Adamic race died in trespasses and sins; they became corrupt in all human faculties. From this conception, “all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

Repentance from sin is a benefit of divine grace; it is supplied by the Word of God and by the work of the Spirit of God. This gift affects man in his mind, emotions, and will. From the standpoint of the mind, sinners become convinced of their guilt, corruption, and offensiveness before God. From the standpoint of their emotions, sinners come to despise their condition and manner of life. From the standpoint of their will, sinners are renewed so that they can turn from their sins and seek a life of obedience to the law of God. This experience is necessary for salvation.
There are three aspects of humanity’s sin. People sin against the majesty (the glory) of God; they sin against the purity of God; they are sinful in the sense of their basic depraved nature.

Sin is an act and/or condition that is the product of the human will. In that consideration, sin is any transgression of God’s law, and it is any failure to conform to God’s nature of purity and goodness. In this light, the Scriptures declare that “all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

Humankind sins against God by failing to recognize the honor and glory of God. The profane use of His name and Word and an irreverent attitude toward His presence is sin. This is illustrated most openly in idolatry, and more subtly in egotism, self-indulgence, dedication to earthly affections more than to God, and selfishness and dependency upon the temporal. Whatever are its forms, this sin is intolerable to God and He will not share His glory with another (Isaiah 42:8).

The sins against God’s purity exist in both act and condition. It is sinful to be in a depraved condition, and it is morally blamable. The absence of the qualities of holiness, justice, goodness, truth, and love cause humankind to be depraved. Conversely, God requires humankind to have these qualities if humanity would be blessed in His presence. It is not only sinful to do things that violate the divine nature; but also it is sinful to be contrary to the divine nature.

The Scriptures describe the depravity of human beings and the sinfulness of their deeds. The Scriptures are very careful to point out that these descriptions are applicable to all humanity: Gentile and Jew. Humanity’s mind is corrupt because there is no understanding of God. People’s wills are corrupt because they have chosen their own way and not God’s way. In their hearts and their words (which are the index of the heart), people are corrupt because they are deceitful, liars, and destructive in their ways. People are destructive and murderous. From the standpoint of religious experience, they are corrupt because there is no fear of God before their eyes. (Note Paul’s citation of Psalm 14:1-3 and Psalm 53:1-3 in Romans 3:9-18.)
The revelation of the sinfulness of humankind shows the necessity and nature of repentance.

Of the nature of repentance, we note the following characteristics. It is the gift of God’s grace, for it is the goodness of God that leads humanity to repentance (Romans 2:4). Humans are dead in trespasses and sins and cannot determine their own repentance; God grants repentance unto life (Acts 11:18). Those who are in sin oppose themselves, and we are to pray that God will give them repentance (2 Timothy 2:25).

As sin is operative in mind, emotions, and will, repentance must also be. From the standpoint of the mind, sinners must hear and learn the law of God. Thus, they become conscious of the condemnation of the law of God and of the wrath of God. They must see the horror of their own sins and their repulsiveness to God and His holiness. They must recognize their own inability to cease from sin (Jeremiah 13:23).

In addition to the law of God, sinners must hear and learn the gospel of God, becoming conscious of God’s mercy in Christ and of God’s renewal of the will of humankind to enable them to cease from sin (Romans 1:16, 17; 10:13-15).

Sinners’ emotional experience in repentance is shown in their hatred of their sinful condition and of their sins. They are reduced to grief and sorrow for their sins; and out of this sorrow, repentance is wrought (2 Corinthians 7:10). This emotional upheaval shows itself in many ways: “What carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!” (2 Corinthians 7:11).

As the nature of sin involves the will, the nature of repentance involves the will. Humankind’s will is totally enslaved to sin (Romans 6:16). The sinner’s will must be strengthened and renewed by the Holy Spirit; so that the sinner wills (wishes) to repent (Psalm 119:59).

Repentance is a complete reversal of life in which sin is forsaken and believers determine to follow God as they once followed sin (Romans 6:17-19). Repentance requires “fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:7-14). This fruit involves the forsaking of the past, restitution of wrongs, confession of sins, and the filling in of the future with new obedience.

The necessity of this experience is borne out by reason and by Scripture. Individuals must know that they are sinners before they will seek to be saved from sin. They must know that they are lost in order to seek a guide. They must know that they are condemned before they will seek forgiveness. They cannot and will not be forgiven until they wish to be.

The Scripture references that demand repentance are abundant and clear. It was the message of the Old Testament prophets (Isaiah 55:7). This was the uncompromising call of both John and Jesus (Matthew 3:2; 4:17). The disciples went forth from Jesus preaching repentance (Mark 6:12). It was the proclamation of the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:38). It was Paul’s demand to the Athenians (Acts 17:30). It is the message of God in the light of the return of our Lord Jesus (2 Peter 3:9).

It is the work of the Holy Spirit to reprove the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment (John 16:7-11). His work and Word are direct confrontations with the world. So His conviction of sin is a moral judgment in which the world is convicted before the holiness of God. The ground of this judgment is that they have not believed on Christ. He also convicts the world concerning righteousness. This also is a moral judgment, and its measure is the righteousness of God. The measure of the righteousness is the life of the Son of God, which we rejected when we put Him to death. The third area of conviction is judgment. This is the announcement that judgment has come. This is primarily the judgment of Satan, the prince of this world. This judgment has already occurred, and it stands as accomplished fact. Since Satan himself is already condemned, his whole world order is also condemned. These are the bases upon which individual conviction of sinners occurs; hence the work of the Holy Spirit is necessary for repentance.
Article 5
We believe that justification, regeneration, and the new birth
are wrought by faith in the blood of Jesus Christ.

We believe that justification is an act of divine judgment in which all the acts of ungodly people are forgiven and they are declared to be righteous in the sight of God. The bases of this declaration of forgiveness and righteousness are the perfection of Christ’s life, the atonement of His death, and the victory of His resurrection. This declaration frees believers from all guilt, relieves them of all judgment, and gives them the full merit of Christ’s obedience to God. The sole instrument of this gift is faith in Jesus Christ as He is revealed in the Word of God.

We believe that adoption is a judicial and personal act of God in which those who were by nature and origin the children of wrath are received into the family of God and are numbered among the children of God. They receive the rights and privileges of the heirs of God and joint heirs of the only begotten Son, Jesus Christ.

We believe that regeneration is a creative act of God through divine grace. In this act of new creation, the Word and Spirit of God implant the seed of life of Christ. The Word and Spirit bring forth in the new birth new creatures in Christ Jesus. They have been created anew in mind, heart, and will. There are three marks of this new creation: (1) the shedding abroad of the love of God in the heart of the believer by the Holy Spirit, (2) the presence of the renewed image of God (manifested by the fruit of the Spirit), and (3) the cessation of the practice of sin.

Justification is God’s act and not humanity’s act. As an act, it is distinct from a work or process; there are no degrees of justification. An individual is either justified or not justified. As God’s gift, it is an act of divine grace. The believer can claim to merit in words, deeds, thoughts, or personal character. God justifies freely by His grace and in His own authority and power: “It is God that justifieth” (Romans 8:33). The operation of God’s grace in justification is declared in Romans 3:24: “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”

There are two aspects of the act of justification. The first is the declaration of forgiveness. The second is the declaration of righteousness. In the declaration of forgiveness, God pardons all the believer’s sins and blots them out of the personal account of the believer. He takes the entire past life of sin and writes “pardoned” across the record. It is the echo of what we hear from the lips of Christ in His encounter with sinners: “Thy sins be forgiven thee” (Mark 2:9).

When God pardons the sinner, He also removes the condemnation. The judgment of God has been fully met and satisfied in the shedding of the blood of Jesus Christ: “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace” (Ephesians 1:7). Justification removes the wrath of God from the sinner: “Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him” (Romans 5:9).

The declaration that we are righteous is essential to our justification. Without this declaration, believers would be in the position of pardoned criminals; though they no longer have their guilt to face, they do not have any merit to offer for themselves. They have no record of righteousness.

They must build a new record of obedience for merit. God declares believers to be righteous by placing on their records the perfection of Christ’s life of obedience to God and fulfillment of the law of God. This record is faultless in holiness and righteousness. It is a record of merit that exactly matches the character of God. With this declaration of righteousness, God also gives the reward of righteousness, which is eternal life.

Adoption is a judicial and personal act of God. As a judicial act, it changes the legal status of the individual. The change of status is to the position of child. It is a personal act of God because it creates an intimate relationship with God in the place of a distant and impersonal relationship with God. As an act, it is distinct from process; it occurs on the authority of God’s decree and with the issuance of God’s Word.

The children of adoption are those who have been justified by God’s grace in Christ (Romans 5:1; 8:1). By nature, we were children of disobedience and wrath (Ephesians 2:1-3). By God’s decree in Christ, we become the children of God: “But when the fullness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Galatians 4:4, 5).

The results of adoption are that we are received into the family of God and that we are made the heirs of God. The position and character of family relationship are represented by the right to call God our Father, even to approach Him with the intimacy of the only begotten Son by praying, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). It is further represented by the fact that we are called children (Romans 8:14-17; Galatians 4:4-6) and that we are joint-heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

The privileges that we receive as children of God are the right and grace to bear God’s name, the gift of His Spirit, access to the throne of grace in prayer, the special love that God has for His children, the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the witness of the Holy Spirit that we are the children of God, the intercession of the Holy Spirit, the provision of God for our well-being, the chastisement of children, the inheritance with Christ, and the promises of everlasting salvation.

Two terms are prominent in Scripture in relation to our new life in Christ: regeneration and the new birth. Both of these terms deal with the fact that humankind’s nature must be changed. In justification and adoption, humanity’s position in relation to God is changed. In regeneration, humanity’s character is changed. Justification and adoption are legal declarations. Regeneration is a creative act of God’s grace.

Regeneration represents a change of origin and a change of nature. The seed of the new birth is the Word of God and the agent of its implanting is the Holy Spirit. In this experience, a new life is implanted which produces the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22, 23). It is the restoration of the image of God in human beings, though not the perfection of that image (Ephesians 4:23; Colossians 3:10). This is specifically the restoration of righteousness and true holiness and the renewal of the mind after the mind of God.

As in other relationships of humanity, we emphasize in this, the mind, emotions, and will. Each of these must be transformed in the producing of the new creature in Christ. The mind is renewed in the image of God. The heart of stone is broken up and in its place there is a heart of flesh on which may be written the law of God and the epistle of Christ (2 Corinthians 3:3). The will is renewed in order that we may “do his will, working in [us] that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ…” (Hebrews 13:21; cf., also Philippians 3:12).

The result of the new birth is a radical change of manner of life. Holiness becomes the disposition of the soul. Love becomes the motive of life. The fruit of the Spirit becomes the characteristic of life. God enables the born-again person to stop the practice of sin.

The instrument by which all these experiences are received is faith in Jesus Christ as He reveals Himself in the written Word of God. The Christ who reveals Himself in His Word is the saving Christ. A faith that is not directed toward the revealing and revealed Christ is not saving faith.

This faith is a denial of human merit; so that human beings abandon any attempt at selfrighteousness and any attempt to earn their position before God. It is an acknowledgement of the believer’s complete dependence upon God for eternal life and for the experiences and provisions of salvation. This faith recognizes the necessity of the Word of God and the Spirit of God in the experiences and assurances of salvation. Such faith is not the product of human persuasion (including self-persuasion), but is a gift of God’s grace (Ephesians 2:8, 9).
We have previously studied the necessity of the blood of Christ for redemption; see the explanation of Article 3 on the death of Christ.
Article 6
We believe in sanctification subsequent to the new birth,
through faith in the blood of Christ; through the Word, and by the Holy Ghost.

Sanctification is an act of divine grace. The Agents of this experience in grace are the Word and Spirit of God. The basis on which God performs this act of grace is the blood of Christ’s atonement. In this act, the body of sin is crucified and all unrighteousness is purged from the heart of the regenerated person. He is thus made free from the law of sin and death, and the graces that have been implanted in the prior experience of regeneration are released to a more fruitful growth by the Holy Spirit.

In saying that sanctification is subsequent to the new birth, we make a distinction between sanctification, justification, regeneration, and adoption. By their very nature, justification, regeneration, and adoption anticipate and point to sanctification. Justification provides the judicial basis for sanctification. Adoption provides the family basis (i.e. family identity) for sanctification. Regeneration provides the basis for sanctification.

Sin is twofold: It is manifested in actual transgressions (commission and omission) of the law of God, and it is manifested in inward corruption and defilement. The sin question cannot be answered until sinners are both forgiven of their sins and have been cleansed from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

Sanctification is separation from the world and sin. This aspect of sanctification occurs by virtue of the fact that we have been joined with Christ. This aspect of sanctification is like ceremonial separation; it occurs because the believer no longer belongs to the world, but belongs to God in Christ.

Sanctification, as a distinctive experience of redemption, deals more significantly with cleansing from sin. Accordingly, such words as “purge,” “cleanse,” “purify,” etc., are prominent in describing this experience in grace. Note the following passages of Scripture.
Psalm 51:7: “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter
than snow.”
John 15:2: “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch
that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.”
1 Corinthians 6:11: “And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified,
but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”

Sanctification is also a crucifying of the body of sin. The Scriptures use various figures of speech and other descriptive terms to define and illustrate this element in man: “old man” (Romans 6:6); “sin that dwelleth in me” (Romans 7:17); “the body of this death” (Romans 7:24); the “flesh” (Romans 7:25); “the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2); the “carnal mind” (Romans 8:7); and others.

The issue of sanctification is dealt with in terms which are appropriate to the terms listed above. It is the crucifixion of the “old man” (Romans 6:6); it is deliverance from the “body of this death” (Romans 7:24); it is being made “free from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2); it is being “spiritually minded” rather than “carnally minded” (Romans 8:6, 7); it is the crucifixion of the world to the believer and of the believer to the world (Galatians 6:14); it is cleansing by the “washing of water by the word” (Ephesians 5:25, 26); it is cleansing from “all filthiness of the flesh and spirit” (2 Corinthians 7:1).

Since these provisions deal with the inward nature and its change, they are accomplishments of divine grace. As an act of divine grace, it is provided for in the Atonement and is accomplished in the believer by the Holy Spirit. The believer is, therefore, sanctified by the blood of Christ: “Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate” (Hebrews 13:12; cf., 1 John 1:7-9). It is accomplished in the crucifixion of Christ (Romans 6:6-8; cf., also John 17:17-19). The Word of God is the spoken and written agent of sanctification (John 17:17); the Holy Spirit is the personal agent in applying the benefits of the Atonement in sanctification (2 Thessalonians 2:13; 1 Peter 1:2).

Sanctification is claimed by an act of faith on the part of believers. They are called on to account (“reckon”) themselves to be dead to sin (Romans 6:11). The believers are “sanctified by faith” (Acts 26:18).
Article 7
We believe holiness to be God’s standard of living for His people.

The pursuit of holy living is the normal manner of life for the believer. This life is characterized by freedom from sinning; by a denial of the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life; by freedom from the law of sin and death; and by the cultivation of the fruit of the Spirit.

The believer is wholly dependent on the Word and Spirit of God as the agents of redemption and of the atoning death of Christ in the pursuit of holiness. Believers are incapable of achieving a holy life through self-discipline, obedience to law or ordinances, self-affliction, or any other device of the flesh.
The expectation of being in Christ is that we should not sin (1 John 2:1; 3:9; John 5:14; 8:11). Paul reasons that those who are dead to sin ought not to live any longer in sin (Romans 6:1, 2).
It is the aim of our spiritual and individual priesthood that we present our bodies as “a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is [our] reasonable service” (Romans 12:1).

The exhortations of Scripture prod the believer to the pursuit of holiness: “Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1). The aim of the believer’s chastening by the Lord is that “we might be partakers of his (God’s) holiness” and that it might produce the “peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Hebrews 12:9-11). These exhortations are climaxed by the strong exhortation: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14).

The love of the world (with its operating techniques of the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life) is the character of the unregenerate; the character of the believer is the love of God and the rejection of this world order (1 John 2:15-17). The conquest over the world and its lusts is an act of faith in Jesus Christ. It is an act of faith in which believers appropriate the crucifixion of the “old man” which was accomplished at the cross (Romans 6:1-6), and in which they consider themselves to be (reckon themselves to be; account themselves to be) dead unto sin and alive unto God (Romans 6:11-16).

The agents for the fulfillment of the life of holiness are the Word and the Spirit of God. In Christ’s description of the vine and His application to the disciples, He said, “Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you” (John 15:3). He appealed to the Word as the sanctifying agent in His high priestly prayer (John 17:17). Growth by the “sincere milk of the word” is essential to the laying aside of evil inward attitudes and works (1 Peter 2:1, 2).

The work of the Holy Spirit is essential if the believer is to be set “free from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2). It is by walking in the Spirit that the believer fulfills the righteousness of the law (Romans 8:3, 4). It is by the Spirit that the deeds of the body are to be put to death (Romans 8:13). It is by walking in the Spirit that the believer is enabled to avoid walking in the flesh (Galatians 5:16). To be led by the Spirit is to be freed from the bondage of the law (Galatians 5:18), and to be led by the Spirit is to produce the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-26).

Three elements remove the pursuit of holiness from the realm of personal achievement [by discipline, the works of the law, religious ceremonies (or ordinances), self-affliction, etc.]. These three elements are faith, the Word, and the Spirit. We have noted these immediately above. Each of these places the center of activity and victory outside the believer and places it in Christ and His crucifixion. It is out of that redemptive crucifixion that the believer is crucified to the world and the world to Him (Galatians 6:14).
Article 8
We believe in the baptism with the Holy Ghost subsequent to a clean heart.

To be baptized with the Holy Spirit is to be filled with the Spirit of God. It is described as an outpouring of the Spirit by which the believer is filled with the presence of the third person of the Trinity, who serves the believer as Paraclete.
This indwelling as Paraclete gives the believer the special enduement of the power of God.
This experience is dependent upon a prior experience of the purification of the heart and is evidence that the believer who receives it has been freed from the law of sin and death.

The Scriptures use the term “baptize” with the Holy Spirit when God poured out His Spirit on the disciples on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4; cf., Acts 1:5). This term is also applicable to the other instances recorded in the Book of Acts where believers received the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14-17; 10:44-48; 19:1-6). A comparison of these passages will show that the terms “baptize,” “give the Spirit,” “pour out the Spirit,” “fill with the Spirit” are equivalent terms.

The special characteristic of this experience is that the believer is filled with the Spirit. In Ephesians 5:18, this concept of being filled with the Spirit stands in contrast to being “drunk with wine.” To be filled with the Spirit is to be brought under the influence of the Spirit of God so that the Spirit governs the personal nature of the believer in mind, emotions, and will.

The Holy Spirit is the personal agent for the revelation of God (1 Corinthians 2:9-11). His various titles in Scripture identify Him as the Spirit of God (Matthew 3:16; 12:28; and many others), the Spirit of your Father (Matthew 10:20), the Spirit of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2; 61:1; Luke 4:18), Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), Spirit of His (God’s) Son (Galatians 4:6). There are many other titles of the Holy Spirit, and many other references that we have not cited above. The special
characteristic of these titles is that they identify the Holy Spirit in His relationship in the Holy Trinity, i.e., in His divine nature.

The experience of the baptism with the Holy Spirit is promised to those who already believe on Jesus Christ for salvation (John 14:15-17). In each of the recorded instances in the Book of Acts in which believers received the Holy Spirit, the recipients were already believers on Christ (Acts 2:1-4; 8:14-17; 9:17; 10:1-6, 34-38, 44-48; 19:1-7). After giving the promise of the Holy Spirit (John 14:16), Christ prayed for the sanctifying of the disciples (John 17). It is the nature of the Holy Spirit to require holiness of those whom He fills (Romans 8:12-14; 1 Corinthians 6:19, 20).
To be filled with the Spirit is to be freed from the law of sin and death (Romans 8:2-4); it is to walk in the Spirit, manifesting the graces of Jesus Christ (Galatians 5:16-25).
Article 9
We believe in speaking with other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance
and that it is the initial evidence of the baptism of the Holy Ghost.

The genuine experience of speaking in tongues is a manifestation of the Holy Spirit. It is a divine-human communication in which the believer speaks in exact response to the mind of the Holy Spirit. Believers are powerless to speak without this responsive relationship with the Holy Spirit and without the Spirit’s movement upon them.

Speaking in tongues in this manner is the initial outward evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit. This experience is the promise of God to every believer. Speaking in tongues by the movement of the Holy Spirit is a continuing ministry of the Holy Spirit.

Speaking in tongues is consistently related to the experience of being filled with the Holy Spirit as reported in the Book of Acts. The initial outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples of Christ is related in these words: “And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4). The special significance of this statement is that the experience of speaking in tongues on the part of the believer was prompted by and provided by the unction of the Holy Spirit, not by the independent action or initiating action of the believer.

While the apostle Peter was preaching to the household of Cornelius, “the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word” (Acts 10:44). Those who had accompanied Peter from Joppa (Acts 10:23, 45) witnessed this experience and they were convinced of the genuineness of this experience by the fact that “they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God” (Acts 10:45, 46). Peter’s companions suggested that these new recipients of the Holy Ghost be baptized in water (Acts 10:47, 48).

The apostle Paul ministered to believers who had followed the preaching of John the Baptist; he enlightened them on the message of Christ, Christian baptism, and the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 19:1-5). The Scriptures further witness: “And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them; and they spake with tongues, and prophesied” (Acts 19:6).

These are not the only occasions recorded in which believers received the Holy Spirit. These, however, do demonstrate the following doctrinal conclusions: (1) speaking in tongues is an experience associated with the baptism in the Holy Spirit; (2) speaking in tongues is an experience initiated by and dependent upon the moving of the Holy Spirit within the believer; (3) speaking in tongues is consistently used by the New Testament church as evidence of the baptism with the Holy Spirit (see Acts 11:15-18).

The Scriptures do not imply that speaking in tongues in and of itself is proof of the infilling of the Holy Spirit. It is an outwardly observable experience which, in conjunction with other evidences, is an assurance to the individual believer and to the church that a brother or sister has received the baptism with the Holy Spirit.

The experience of the baptism with the Holy Spirit is the will of God for every believer. It was so promised in the Old Testament prophecy of Joel 2:28-32; this is cited by Peter on the Day of Pentecost: “And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh…” (Acts 2:17). Peter associated this experience with the continuing extension of the gospel: “Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call” (Acts 2:38, 39).

The continuation of the experience of speaking in tongues by the power of the Holy Spirit is evidenced in the instructions that are given to the Corinthians. There is a ministry of the Holy Spirit in giving “various kinds of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:10). The Holy Spirit gives a ministry of tongues which must be interpreted also by the ministry of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 14:13, 27, 28); He also gives a ministry of tongues which is a mysterious communion between the believer and God (1 Corinthians 14:2, 14, 15, 27, 28). Paul’s understanding in all of these instructions is that these provisions are for all believers in all ages of the church: “I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather ye prophesied: for greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying” (1 Corinthians 14:5). The ministry of tongues continues in the worship experiences of the believer: “What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also” (1 Corinthians 14:15).
Article 10
We believe in water baptism by immersion, and all who repent should be
baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.

Water baptism is a sacrament (ordinance) which was ordained by our Lord Jesus Christ while He was with us in the flesh (Matthew 28:19, 20). This sacrament is administered by the church in obedience to Christ’s commission. The aim of the sacrament is to represent the believer’s entrance into the kingdom of God through regeneration. The visible symbols of the sacrament are the water of baptism (Acts 10:47) and the physical act of immersion (Colossians 2:11, 12).

In water baptism, the element of water represents the washing of regeneration by the Word and by the blood of Christ. The act of immersion represents the believer’s death, burial, and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3-5; Colossians 2:11, 12). Baptism thereby witnesses to the believer’s death to sin and resurrection to newness of life in the pursuit of holiness.

The sacrament of water baptism is Christ’s ordained witness to the believer’s repentance and to the new life in Christ (Acts 9:17, 19). Though the ceremony does not have regenerating power, it is a vital means of grace and it is a sign and seal of God’s work of regeneration.

Christ has given specific commandment that believers receive this rite (Matthew 28:19, 20). It is, therefore, important as an act of obedience to Christ (1 Peter 3:21) and for the receiving of the spiritual benefits that the Holy Spirit imparts in the experience (Galatians 3:27). The words by which Christ ordained this sacrament are the only acceptable verbal formula to be used in the administration of the sacrament. Therefore, water baptism is to be administered “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Matthew 28:19).

Our Lord Jesus ordained the rite of baptism. Its clearest statement of ordination is the Great Commission: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.” (Matthew 28:19, 20). The early church observed this rite both in its exhortations to believers (Acts 2:38) and in its practices in evangelism (Acts 8:12; 10:48). It is significant that in all of the sacramental practices of the New Testament period of the church, the church did not create any ordinance either by its own decision or by the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

Sacraments are designed to portray religious experience. The sacrament of baptism is designed to depict the following experiences in Christ: the new birth, cleansing, death to sin, burial, and resurrection to a new life. Therefore, all of the elements of the ceremony are important. In order to represent cleansing, water is appropriate. Ananias exhorted Saul of Tarsus to be baptized and, as he did, he related the cleansing of water as the symbol for the washing away of sin: “And now why tarriest thou? Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord” (Acts 22:16). In order to represent death, burial, and resurrection, immersion is appropriate: “In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the

body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ: Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead: (Colossians 2:11, 12). In order to represent the new birth, the coming forth from the water into a new life is appropriate: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection” (Romans 6:4, 5).

The temporal agent for God in the administering of this ordinance is the church. The church is subject to error in its judgment; so, its administering of the sacrament is not an assurance of salvation. It is an acknowledgment by the church that the body of believers accepts the testimony of the one who is being baptized: “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41). Note also the order of testimony and baptism in the experience of the Philippian jailor: “And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house…And he (the jailor) took them the same hour of the night and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway” (Acts 16:31-33). On the part of the believer, baptism is “the answer of a good conscience toward God” (1 Peter 3:21).

The experience of being baptized in water does not regenerate; however, it is spiritually related to our baptism into the body of Christ: “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). This experience enforces and strengthens our baptism into the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13) and our baptism into death (Romans 6:4).

The verbal formula of baptism is important in the observance of Christ’s institution of the sacrament and for the doctrinal significance of the words. The correct verbal formula for Christian baptism is contained in the words of Christ in the Apostolic Commission: “…in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Matthew 28:19). (We recognize that the record of the Book of Acts uses expressions of Christ’s authority to save and to order baptism: note Acts 8:16; 10:47, 48; 19:5. We do not see in these instances a violation of the formula in Matthew 28:19; instead, we see an affirmation of Christ’s command. To baptize in Christ’s name is to baptize as he instructed.)
In doctrinal significance, these words worship the triune God and recognize the work of each individual person of the Trinity in redemption.
Article 11
We believe divine healing is provided for all in the atonement.

The death of Christ is the Atonement for man’s sins. It is also the redemption of the whole man: body, soul, and spirit. This act of redemption not only provides freedom from sin, but also for the judicial consequences of sin, including the infirmities of the flesh.
The healing of the body is provided by the atonement of Christ (Isaiah 53:4, 5; Matthew 8:16, 17; 1 Peter 2:24). This healing is administered through divine intervention.

The present condition of humankind is the product of humanity’s sin; sin violated God’s moral law, and it violated God’s laws of nature. Therefore, the consequences of humanity’s sin are spiritual depravity and alienation and bodily corruption and death.

In all ages of His revelation of Himself to humanity, God has related the message of deliverance from sin to the message of healing. In delivering Israel from Egypt and in making redemptive covenant with them, God promised, “If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the Lord thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I brought upon the Egyptians…” (Exodus 15:26). The basis of this promise is “I am the Lord that healeth thee.”
The going forth of the Word of God is the going forth of healing: “He sent his word, and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions” (Psalm 107:20).

The relationship between forgiveness and healing is clearly stated in the praise of the psalmist: “Bless the Lord, O my soul...Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases” (Psalm 103:1-3).

The provision of healing on the basis of the redemptive work of the Messiah is clearly stated. Jesus interpreted His ministry of healing to be a fulfillment of Isaiah 29:18: “And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness.” His answer to John the Baptist’s inquiry appealed to the healing of the blind, the lame, the lepers, the deaf, and the raising of the dead (Matthew 8:16, 17).

The relationship of healing to Atonement is stated by Peter: “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed” (1 Peter 2:24). This is inspired commentary on Isaiah 53:5: “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”

God ministers healing within the covenant by various means. He ministers healing by the gifts of the Holy Spirit: faith, healing, and miracles (1 Corinthians 12:9, 10). He ministers healing through prayer, the laying on of hands, the anointing with oil, faith, and the confession of sin:

“Is any sick among you? Let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him. Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:14-16).
Article 12
We believe in the Lord’s Supper and washing of the saints’ feet.

The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament ordained by our Lord Jesus Christ while He was with us in the flesh. In the instituting of this rite, He ordained the use of the following visible elements: bread and the fruit of the vine. The setting in which He established this ordinance was a meal. The aim of the sacrament is to represent and communicate spiritual nourishment in Christ to the believer.
By the bread, the sacrament represents the body of Christ broken for us in redemption. The poured wine represents the blood of Christ shed as the seal of the new covenant for the remission of sins.

By the eating of the bread and the drinking of the wine, the believer is, by symbol and faith, partaking of the body and blood of Jesus for spiritual nurture. This sacrament is also a memorial of Christ’s life, death, and resurrection. It is also an anticipation of His return.

The agent for the administering of this sacrament is the church. The body of Christ is His ordained witness of the believers’ continuance in Him, nurture by Him, and fellowship in His body. It is a vital means by which the Holy Spirit cultivates spiritual graces and strength in the believer. The observance and repetition of this sacred meal are essential to obedience and spiritual nurture.

The words by which Christ instituted this rite are the only authorization that the church has for administering it and claiming its benefits by faith. These words and elements of the Supper alone are sufficient for the offering of this holy meal. No other audible and visible signs are needed.

The washing of the saints’ feet is a sacrament ordained by our Lord Jesus Christ while He was with us in the flesh. The aim of this ordinance is to represent the believers’ continuing union with Christ, purification by Him, and servanthood to others in the body of Christ.

By the element of water, the rite represents the washing of those who are in Christ. The act of washing the feet is an act of servanthood; this ordinance, therefore, symbolizes believers’ subjection to one another. This ordinance is a vital means of grace in the perpetuation of spiritual purification and in the fellowship of servants.

By its nature, the Lord’s Supper is a meal; it is, therefore, an appropriate symbol of nourishment. The bread is a representation of the body of Christ: “And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26; cf., Mark 14:22; Luke 22:19). The act of breaking the bread represents the crucifixion of our Lord and the provision for spiritual nurture out of the sacrificial meal: “For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:23, 24).

The beverage—the fruit of the vine—is a representation of the blood of Christ shed in sacrifice: “And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it (drink all ye of it); For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:27, 28; cf., Mark 14:23, 24; Luke 22:20).

The pouring of the wine represents the shedding of Christ’s blood in His crucifixion and the provision of spiritual nurture through this sacrificial meal; it is also a dramatization of the crucifixion scene so that we reexperience Calvary spiritually: “After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do show the Lord’s death till he come” (1 Corinthians 11:25, 26). The emphasis on nurture is also contained in Paul’s exhortation: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16).

The prominent elements in this sacred meal are spiritual nurture in partaking of the body and blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16, 17, 21); a memorial and recollection of the death of our Lord (Matthew 26:26-29; Mark 14:22-25; Luke 22:19, 20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26); and an expectation of Christ’s return when believers will partake with Him in the heavenly meal. Our Lord emphasized this aspect of the celebration in His words: “But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29; cf., Mark 14:25).
By its nature, the washing of feet is a cleansing act and it is also the act of a servant. The Lord Jesus instituted this sacrament by His own example of washing the feet of the disciples (John 13:4-
17) and by His specific command: “If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also

ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you” (John 13:14, 15). It is also evident that this practice continued in the observances of the early church (1 Timothy 5:10).

Our Lord, by words and example, gave this ordinance symbolic redemptive significance. First, He warned Peter of the haughtiness by which he rejected Jesus’ offer to wash his feet: “Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me” (John 13:8). Second, Jesus attached the significance of the rite to purification. Peter’s overly zealous response to Jesus’ rebuke was his offer: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head” (John 13:9). Then, Jesus showed the symbolic character of the cleansing sacramentally in the washing of feet: “Jesus saith to him, He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit: and ye are clean, but not all” (John 13:10).

Our Lord also gave this ordinance the significance of fellowship and communion. The mutuality of the act of washing one another’s feet is a bond of fellowship in which masters and servants exchange roles and demonstrate that all leadership in the body of Christ is a leadership of servanthood. Our Lord demonstrated His lordship by being a servant in the task of washing the feet of His disciples.

Both the Lord’s Supper and the washing of the saints’ feet are repetitive sacraments. The need for nourishment is constant in the life of the believer; therefore, the partaking of the Lord’s body and blood by faith is a continual need. The anticipation of the Lord’s return should be frequently in the mind and anticipation of believers; so, the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper should frequently remind us of His coming. It is urgent that we go often to Calvary and that we be renewed frequently by observing Holy Communion.

The need for cleansing of the heart is continual; the flow of Christ’s blood provides for the believer the assurance of purification: “But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:7).

It is important that both of these sacraments be protected from unbiblical embellishments; therefore, we urge that the words of institution and the elements named in Scripture for the observance of them are the only visible and audible elements needed for their proper observance.
Article 13
We believe in the premillennial second coming of Jesus. First,
to resurrect the righteous dead and to catch away the living saints
to Him in the air. Second, to reign on the earth a thousand years.

The second coming of Jesus Christ is the personal, literal, and bodily return of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to earth. As the Son of God and as the Son of David, He will reign on earth for one thousand years—the Millennium.
In the affirmation of the “premillennial second coming of Jesus Christ,” we affirm that the return of Christ is necessary before the millennial reign can take place.

The first purpose of Christ’s second advent is the glorification of all believers. The dead in Christ will be raised from the dead in the likeness of Christ’s bodily resurrection. Theirs will be a literal, bodily resurrection. Those believers in Christ who are alive, in the flesh, at the time of Christ’s return will be translated into the likeness of Christ’s resurrected body. Theirs will be a literal, bodily translation and transformation into immortality. The order of this event is that the dead in Christ will be raised first; then, the believers who are alive in the flesh will be caught up to be with the Lord. All saints receive the same transformation into immortality and incorruption, and they are all united together with Christ.

The second purpose of the Second Coming is for Christ to establish a reign of peace on earth by His binding of Satan for a thousand years, and by His personal, physical presence in the world, and rulership of all of its inhabitants, elements, and energies.

In this article of faith, we refer to the second coming of Christ as that event in which He personally appears, raptures His saints, reigns on earth for 1,000 years, judges all mankind, and finally establishes the eternal Kingdom. The predominant emphasis of this article, however, is Christ’s coming to receive His saints and to establish the earthly reign, or millennium.

The second coming of Christ is His personal return, as distinct from the coming of Christ through the presence of the Holy Spirit. Jesus distinctly separated these two promises. He promised His personal return. The object of this return is that we may abide with Him in our Father’s house forever: “In my Father’s house are many mansions: If it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also” (John 14:2, 3). Subsequent to this saying and in distinction from this promise, Christ also promised the sending of the Holy Spirit (John 16:7; cf., John 14:16-26). It is clear that the coming of the Holy Spirit and the presence of the Holy Spirit are not to be understood as the return or presence of Christ.
The return of Christ is literal; it is a bodily return as His ascension was:

And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. And while they looked steadfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel; Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? This same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven (Acts 1:9-11).

The ascension of Christ here is made the pattern by which we are to expect Christ’s return. He ascended bodily; He will return bodily. He ascended into heaven; He will return from heaven. His ascension was accompanied by angels; His return will be accompanied by angels. Our Lord, in His words to the apostles, associated His return with His departure. See John 14:2, 3 cited above.

Christ’s return will be visible to those of faith and to those of unbelief.
